arXiv:1707.04043v1 [math.AP] 13 Jul 2017

Quasi-steady state reduction for the Michaelis-Menten reaction-diffusion system

Martin Frank Note: MathCCES, RWTH Aachen, 52056 Aachen, Germany    Christian Lax Note: Lehrstuhl A f. Mathematik, RWTH Aachen, 52056 Aachen, Germany    Sebastian Walcher††footnotemark: Note: Corresponding author: walcher@matha.rwth-aachen.de    Olaf Wittich††footnotemark:
Abstract

The Michaelis-Menten mechanism is probably the best known model for an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. For spatially homogeneous concentrations, QSS reductions are well known, but this is not the case when chemical species are allowed to diffuse. We will discuss QSS reductions for both the irreversible and reversible Michaelis-Menten reaction in the latter case, given small initial enzyme concentration and slow diffusion. Our work is based on a heuristic method to obtain an ordinary differential equation which admits reduction by Tikhonov-Fenichel theory. We will not give convergence proofs but we provide numerical results that support the accuracy of the reductions.
MSC2010: 92C45, 34E15, 80A32, 35B40
Keywords: reaction-diffusion equations, enzyme, singular perturbations

1 Introduction

The Michaelis-Menten mechanism [19] is probably the best known model for an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. In this reaction network, a substrate SS and an enzyme EE combine to form a complex CC, which degrades back to substrate and enzyme, or to product P and enzyme. In the reversible setting there is also a back reaction combining EE and PP to complex. The reaction scheme thus reads

E+S→k1→k−1C→k2→k−2E+P.E+S\mathrel{\raisebox{-0.44481pt}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.0pt}{${\mathrel{\to}^{k_{1}}_{\hphantom{k_{-1}}}}$}\hss}\hbox{${\mathrel{\to}^{\hphantom{k_{1}}}_{k_{-1}}}$}}}C\mathrel{\raisebox{-0.44481pt}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.0pt}{${\mathrel{\to}^{k_{2}}_{\hphantom{k_{-2}}}}$}\hss}\hbox{${\mathrel{\to}^{\hphantom{k_{2}}}_{k_{-2}}}$}}}E+P.

In the irreversible case one assumes that product and enzyme cannot combine to form complex, i.e. one has C→k2E+PC\xrightarrow{k_{2}}E+P. Typically, no complex or product are assumed present initially. Assuming mass action kinetics and spatially homogeneous concentrations, the evolution of the concentrations (s,e,c,p)(s,e,c,p) of S,E,C,PS,E,C,P can be described by a system of four ordinary differential equations, from which by stoichiometry one obtains a two-dimensional system (first discussed from a mathematical perspective by Briggs and Haldane [4]). Employing the familiar quasi-steady state (QSS) assumption for complex, based on small initial concentration of enzyme, further reduces the system to dimension one.
For reaction systems, quasi-steady state (QSS) assumptions frequently lead to singular perturbation problems for which the classical theories of Tikhonov [24] and Fenichel [7] are applicable. (Moreover, one should note results by Hoppensteadt [13] on unbounded time intervals; see also [17].)
For spatially inhomogeneous concentrations in a reaction vessel, thus for reaction-diffusion systems, Tikhonov’s and Fenichel’s theory is not applicable since their fundamental results are limited to finite dimensional systems. Therefore, reaction-diffusion systems are much more difficult to analyze, and only partial results are known. As for the Michaelis-Menten reaction with diffusion and small initial enzyme concentration, Britton [5] and Yannacopoulos et al. [25] derived QSS reductions with the additional assumptions of immobile complex and enzyme. Kalachev et al. [14] used asymptotic expansions with respect to a small parameter to obtain results about the behavior of the solutions under different time scales for diffusion, with the diffusion time scale different from the time scale for the slow reaction part. (As [14] indicates, even finding candidates for reduced reaction-diffusion systems may be a nontrivial task.) Starting from different assumptions about the reaction mechanism (viz., smallness of certain rate constants), Bothe and Pierre [2] as well as Bisi et al. [1] discussed reductions for a related system, including convergence proofs.
In the present paper we will discuss QSS reductions for both the irreversible and the reversible Michaelis-Menten reaction with diffusion, under the conditions of small initial enzyme concentration and slow diffusion. Our work is based on a heuristic method described in [8], which utilizes a spatial discretization to obtain an ordinary differential equation which admits reduction by Tikhonov-Fenichel theory. In many relevant cases, the reduced ODE system can, in turn, be identified as the spatial discretization of another partial differential equation system. This resulting PDE is a candidate for the reduced system and, as pointed out in [8], it is the only possible candidate. In the present paper we will not discuss convergence issues, which seem to be quite technically involved, but we provide numerical simulations that support the accuracy of the reduction.
The plan of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we will briefly recall the most important aspects of the spatially homogeneous system and moreover note some general features of the inhomogeneous case.
In Section 3 the “classical” QSS assumption is discussed, i.e. we assume small initial enzyme concentration and slow diffusion. We first review some relevant results from the literature, and give an informal description of the reduction procedure from [8]. Following a (degenerate) scaling similar to the one in Heineken, Tsuchiya and Aris [12] we derive a reduction via the approach in [8]; to the authors’ knowledge, the form of the reduced PDE system has not been known in the literature to date.
The reduction is consistent with the spatially homogeneous case, thus setting the diffusion constants equal to zero yields the usual Michaelis-Menten equation. The degenerate scaling seems unavoidable in the PDE case (while one can circumvent it for the ODE), thus we need to go beyond the classical singular perturbation reduction due to Tikhonov and Fenichel. The scaling requires a consistency condition which is intuitively likely to hold in general; we can justify it mathematically in the case when enzyme and complex diffuse at the same rate. In Section 4 we present numerical simulations which exhibit very good agreement with the reduced system.
In the Appendix, employing the heuristic method from [8], we carry out the necessary computations for the reductions and also determine suitable initial values for the reduced system.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 The spatially homogeneous setting

We recall some facts about the Michaelis-Menten reaction with homogeneously distributed concentrations. The evolution of the concentrations (s,e,c,p)(s,e,c,p) of S,E,C,PS,E,C,P is governed by the four-dimensional ordinary differential equation

s˙=−k1​e​s+k−1​c\displaystyle\dot{s}=-k_{1}es+k_{-1}c
e˙=−k1​e​s+(k−1+k2)​c−k−2​e​p\displaystyle\dot{e}=-k_{1}es+(k_{-1}+k_{2})c-k_{-2}ep
c˙=k1​e​s−(k−1+k2)​c+k−2​e​p\displaystyle\dot{c}=k_{1}es-(k_{-1}+k_{2})c+k_{-2}ep
p˙=k2​c−k−2​e​p.\displaystyle\dot{p}=k_{2}c-k_{-2}ep.

This system admits the (stoichiometric) first integrals Ψ1​(s,e,c,p)=e+c\Psi_{1}(s,e,c,p)=e+c and Ψ2​(s,e,c,p)=s+c+p\Psi_{2}(s,e,c,p)=s+c+p. Therefore a two-dimensional system remains:

s˙=−k1​e0​s+(k1​s+k−1)​c\displaystyle\dot{s}=-k_{1}e_{0}s+(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c (2.1)
c˙=k1​e0​s−(k1​s+k−1+k2)​c+k−2​(e0−c)​(s0−s−c),\displaystyle\dot{c}=k_{1}e_{0}s-(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})c+k_{-2}(e_{0}-c)(s_{0}-s-c), (2.2)

where s0s_{0} and e0e_{0} are the initial concentrations of SS and EE, and initially no product PP or complex CC are present. The system is called irreversible whenever k−2=0k_{-2}=0, and reversible otherwise. The most common quasi-steady state assumption is that the initial enzyme concentration is small, one considers e0=ε​e0∗e_{0}=\varepsilon e_{0}^{*} in the asymptotic limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, for the irreversible system.
Heineken, Tsuchiya and Aris [12] were the first to discuss the Michaelis-Menten system from the perspective of singular perturbations, and Segel and Slemrod [22] were the first to directly prove a rigorous convergence result for the unbounded time interval: Writing (2.1)–(2.2) in the slow time scale τ=ε​t\tau=\varepsilon t

s′=−k1​s​e0∗+ε−1​(k1​s+k−1)​c\displaystyle s^{\prime}=-k_{1}se_{0}^{*}+\varepsilon^{-1}(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c (2.3)
c′=k1​s​e0∗−ε−1​(k1​s+k−1+k2)​c,\displaystyle c^{\prime}=k_{1}se_{0}^{*}-\varepsilon^{-1}(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})c, (2.4)

the solutions of (2.3)–(2.4) converge for all t0>0t_{0}>0 uniformly on [t0,∞)[t_{0},\infty) to the solutions of

s′=−k1​k2​s​e0∗k1​s+k−1+k2s^{\prime}=-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}se_{0}^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}} (2.5)

on the asymptotic slow manifold 𝒱={(s,0),s≥0}\mathcal{V}=\{(s,0),\ s\geq 0\} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. (Below we will sometimes change between time scales without mentioning this explicitly.)
Both the approach by Heineken et al. [12] and the proof by Segel and Slemrod [22] use appropriate scalings of the variables, in particular they introduce z:=c/e0z:=c/e_{0}. It is possible to avoid such a scaling, which becomes degenerate as e0→0e_{0}\to 0, in the spatially homogeneous case (see e.g. [9]) but as it turns out we will need to utilize such a degenerate scaling to obtain a reduction when concentrations are not homogeneously distributed in the reaction vessel.
We will also discuss the reversible Michaelis-Menten system, which appears less frequently in the literature; in part this may be due to the unwieldy expression for the QSS reduction; see Miller and Alberty [20]. The singular perturbation reduction (see [21] and [11]) of (2.3)–(2.4) for k−2>0k_{-2}>0 and e0=ε​e0∗e_{0}=\varepsilon e_{0}^{*} leads to

s′=−(k1​k2​s+k−1​k−2​(s−s0))​e0∗k1​s+k−2​(s0−s)+k−1+k2s^{\prime}=-\frac{(k_{1}k_{2}s+k_{-1}k_{-2}(s-s_{0}))e_{0}^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}(s_{0}-s)+k_{-1}+k_{2}} (2.6)

on the asymptotic slow manifold 𝒱={(s,0),s≥0}\mathcal{V}=\{(s,0),\ s\geq 0\} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. (Here, uniform convergence again holds on [t0,∞)[t_{0},\infty); see [17]). Both the QSS and the singular perturbation reductions agree up to first order in the small parameter; see [11].

2.2 The spatially inhomogeneous setting

When the concentrations are inhomogeneously distributed and diffusion is present then the system is described by a reaction-diffusion equation. Thus, let Ω\Omega be a bounded region with a smooth boundary and let δs,δe,δc,δp≥0\delta_{s},\delta_{e},\delta_{c},\delta_{p}\geq 0 denote the diffusion constants. The governing equations are

∂ts\displaystyle\partial_{t}s =δs​Δ​s−k1​s​e+k−1​c,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}\Delta s-k_{1}se+k_{-1}c, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (2.7)
∂te\displaystyle\partial_{t}e =δe​Δ​e−k1​s​e+(k−1+k2)​c−k−2​e​p,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}\Delta e-k_{1}se+(k_{-1}+k_{2})c-k_{-2}ep, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (2.8)
∂tc\displaystyle\partial_{t}c =δc​Δ​c+k1​s​e−(k−1+k2)​c+k−2​e​p,\displaystyle=\delta_{c}\Delta c+k_{1}se-(k_{-1}+k_{2})c+k_{-2}ep, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (2.9)
∂tp\displaystyle\partial_{t}p =δp​Δ​p+k2​c−k−2​e​p,\displaystyle=\delta_{p}\Delta p+k_{2}c-k_{-2}ep, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (2.10)

with continuous initial values

s(0,x)=s0(x),e(0,x)=e0(x),c(0,x)=c0(x),p(0,x)=p0(x),in Ωs(0,x)=s_{0}(x),\quad e(0,x)=e_{0}(x),\quad c(0,x)=c_{0}(x),\quad p(0,x)=p_{0}(x),\quad\text{in }\Omega

and one has Neumann boundary conditions

∂s∂ν=∂e∂ν=∂c∂ν=∂p∂ν=0,in ​(0,∞)×∂Ω\frac{\partial s}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial e}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial p}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega

with ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} denoting the outer normal derivative. We collect a few general properties.

3 Reduction given slow diffusion and small initial enzyme concentration

3.1 Review of results in the literature

As noted above, there exists no counterpart to Tikhonov’s and Fenichel’s theorems for infinite dimensional systems, hence the reduction of reaction-diffusion equations is not possible in a similarly direct manner.
Regarding the reduction of the Michaelis-Menten reaction with diffusion, one sometimes finds the one-dimensional equation (2.5) augmented by a diffusion term for substrate, with no further argument given. This ad-hoc method is problematic, since it amounts to ignoring diffusion in the reduction step. The appropriate approach is to start with the full system (2.7)–(2.10) and consider possible reductions in the limiting case of small initial concentration for enzyme, with slow diffusion. This will be the vantage point in the present paper.
With regard to such an approach, the authors are aware only of three papers for the irreversible system (i.e. (2.7)–(2.9) with k−2=0k_{-2}=0). Yannacopoulos et al. [25] assumed PP and CC to be immobile (i.e. δe=δc=0\delta_{e}=\delta_{c}=0; see their equation (71)) and gave a second order approximation for the case of a one dimensional domain (see in particular equation (80) which in lowest order reduces to the Michaelis-Menten equation for substrate, augmented by diffusion). Britton [5], Ch. 8 gave the first order approximation

∂τs=δs​Δ​s−k1​k2​s​(e0+c0)k1​s+k−1+k2\partial_{\tau}s=\delta_{s}\Delta s-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}s{(e_{0}+c_{0})}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}} (3.1)

which is in agreement with the lowest order terms given in [25]. He made no assumptions on diffusion constants for enzyme or complex, and instead started with system (2.1)–(2.2), augmented by diffusive terms for ss and cc. This is problematic because the elimination of ee via stoichiometry is no longer possible when diffusion is present. Therefore Britton’s approach is limited to the case considered by Yannacopoulos at al. [25].
Kalachev et al. [14] started from (2.7)–(2.9) and considered up to three time scales, with the slow reaction part of order ε\varepsilon (the total initial mass of enzyme divided by the total initial mass of substrate), a fast reaction part, and diffusion of order δ\delta, deriving asymptotic expansions for the solutions and reductions in different time regimes. They did not discuss the case that slow reaction and diffusion are in the same time scale (i.e., δ=ε\delta=\varepsilon) which we will consider. (In [14], Remark 1.2 further work was announced for this case, but apparently this has not been published yet.)

3.2 Informal review of the reduction heuristics

We will employ a heuristic method to construct a candidate for a reduced system that was introduced in [8]. In contrast to the convergence property for the ODE after discretization (which is a consequence of Tikhonov’s and Fenichel’s theorems) we will not prove convergence here; generally this seems a very hard task (see Section 5). However, as remarked in [8], Proposition 4.3, the reduced PDE determined by the heuristics represents the only possible reduction of the reaction-diffusion system as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.
Briefly the heuristics can be described as follows: By spatial discretization of a reaction-diffusion system which depends on a small parameter ε\varepsilon, one obtains a system of ordinary differential equations depending on ε\varepsilon. If the ODE system admits a Tikhonov-Fenichel reduction and the reduced ODE is the spatial discretization of another partial differential equation system, then we will call the latter the reduced PDE of the reaction-diffusion system. (The conditions stated above are frequently satisfied; see e.g.[16].) The following results are in part based on the second author’s doctoral thesis [16]. Detailed computations will be presented in the Appendix.

3.3 The irreversible case

In order to determine the reduced PDE systems, we need some preparations. We consider first the irreversible reaction-diffusion system (2.7)–(2.9). Defining total enzyme concentration y:=e+cy:=e+c, we get

∂ts\displaystyle\partial_{t}s =δs​Δ​s−k1​s​(y−c)+k−1​c,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}\Delta s-k_{1}s(y-c)+k_{-1}c, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.2)
∂tc\displaystyle\partial_{t}c =δc​Δ​c+k1​s​(y−c)−(k−1+k2)​c,\displaystyle=\delta_{c}\Delta c+k_{1}s(y-c)-(k_{-1}+k_{2})c, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.3)
∂ty\displaystyle\partial_{t}y =δc​Δ​c+δe​(Δ​y−Δ​c),\displaystyle=\delta_{c}\Delta c+\delta_{e}(\Delta y-\Delta c), in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.4)

with initial values s​(0,x)=s0​(x)s(0,x)=s_{0}(x), c​(0,x)=c0​(x)c(0,x)=c_{0}(x), y⁡(0,x)=e0​(x)+c0​(x)y(0,x)=e_{0}(x)+c_{0}(x). Our basic assumptions are:

  • •

    Diffusion is slow, and therefore we introduce the scaling

    δz=ε​δz∗​ for ​z=s,e,c.\delta_{z}=\varepsilon\delta_{z}^{*}\text{ for }z=s,e,c.
  • •

    Total enzyme concentration is small for all t≥0t\geq 0, and therefore we set

    y=ε​y∗​ and ​c=ε​c∗, and also ​e0=ε​e0∗,c0=ε​c0∗.y=\varepsilon y^{*}{\text{ and }c=\varepsilon c^{*}},\text{ and also }e_{0}=\varepsilon e_{0}^{*},\quad c_{0}=\varepsilon c_{0}^{*}.

Incorporating these assumptions we have

∂ts\displaystyle\partial_{t}s =ε​δs∗​Δ​s+ε⁡(k1​s+k−1)​c∗−ε​k1​s​y∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s+\varepsilon(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c^{*}-\varepsilon k_{1}sy^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega
∂tc∗\displaystyle\partial_{t}c^{*} =ε​δc∗​Δ​c−(k1​s+k−1+k2)​c∗+k1​s​y∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{c}^{*}\Delta c-(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})c^{*}+k_{1}sy^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega
∂ty∗\displaystyle\partial_{t}y^{*} =ε​δe∗​Δ​y∗+ε⁡(δc∗−δe∗)​Δ​c∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\varepsilon(\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*})\Delta c^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega

with initial values

s⁡(0,x)=s0​(x),c∗​(0,x)=c0∗​(x),y∗​(0,x)=y0∗​(x):=e0∗​(x)+c0∗​(x).s(0,x)=s_{0}(x),\quad c^{*}(0,x)=c_{0}^{*}(x),\quad y^{*}(0,x)=y^{*}_{0}(x):=e_{0}^{*}(x)+c_{0}^{*}(x).

In slow time τ=ε​t\tau=\varepsilon t one now finds

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s+(k1​s+k−1)​c∗−k1​s​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s+(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c^{*}-k_{1}sy^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.5)
∂τc∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}c^{*} =δc∗​Δ​c∗−ε−1​(k1​s+k−1+k2)​c∗+ε−1​k1​s​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{c}^{*}\Delta c^{*}-\varepsilon^{-1}(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})c^{*}+\varepsilon^{-1}k_{1}sy^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.6)
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗+δ​Δ​c∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\delta\Delta c^{*}, in ​(0,∞)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,\infty)\times\Omega (3.7)

with the abbreviation

δ:=δc∗−δe∗.\delta:=\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*}. (3.8)

We will discuss two different cases: If the diffusion constants δe∗\delta_{e}^{*} and δc∗\delta_{c}^{*} are close in the sense that δ=ε​δ∗\delta=\varepsilon\delta^{*}, then equation (3.7) reads

∂τy∗=δe∗​Δ​y∗+ε​δ∗​Δ​c\partial_{\tau}y^{*}=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\varepsilon\delta^{*}\Delta c (3.9)

and the reduced system for ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is again a reaction-diffusion system (with a rational reaction term). Otherwise, the reduced system becomes highly nonlinear.

Remark 2.

The argument is based on the critical assumption that the “degenerate” scalings c∗=ε−1​cc^{*}=\varepsilon^{-1}c and y∗=ε−1​yy^{*}=\varepsilon^{-1}y hold for all t≥0t\geq 0; to state it more precisely, one needs a uniform bound (with respect to ε\varepsilon) for c∗c^{*} and y∗y^{*}. In the special case δc∗=δe∗\delta_{c}^{*}=\delta_{e}^{*} (e.g. if the molecules of enzyme and complex are of the same size; see Keener and Sneyd [15], Subsection 2.2.2), Remark 1 implies that c∗c^{*} and y∗y^{*} are uniformly bounded by e0∗+c0∗e_{0}^{*}+c_{0}^{*}. We are not able to extend this property to the case δc∗≠δe∗\delta_{c}^{*}\neq\delta_{e}^{*}, but we will verify in the Appendix that the corresponding uniform boundedness property holds for the ODEs obtained via discretization. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that degenerate scaling poses no problem for the Michaelis-Menten system (see Section 4).

3.3.1 Irreversible case with δc∗−δe∗=𝒪⁡(ε)\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)

In this case the reduced PDE (as defined in subsection 3.2) is given by

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s−k1​k2​y∗​sk1​s+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}y^{*}s}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.10)
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.11)

on the asymptotic slow manifold

𝒱={(s,c∗,y∗)∈ℝ+3,c∗=k1​s​y∗k1​s+k−1+k2}.\mathcal{V}=\left\{(s,c^{*},y^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{+},\ c^{*}=\frac{k_{1}sy^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\right\}.

Appropriate initial values on 𝒱\mathcal{V} are given by (s~0,y~0∗)=(s0,y0∗)(\tilde{s}_{0},\tilde{y}_{0}^{*})=\left(s_{0},y_{0}^{*}\right). This assertion is a direct consequence of Proposition A.3 in the Appendix.
Total enzyme concentration in the reduced equation is subject only to diffusion, and there remains a reaction-diffusion equation for substrate, with the reaction part similar to the usual Michaelis-Menten term. It is worth looking at some special cases: When δe∗=δc∗=0\delta_{e}^{*}=\delta_{c}^{*}=0, y∗=y0∗y^{*}=y_{0}^{*} is constant in time and we have

∂τs=δs​Δ​s−k1​k2​s0​y0∗k1​s+k−1+k2\partial_{\tau}s=\delta_{s}\Delta s-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}s_{0}y_{0}^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}

as in Yannacopoulos et al. [25], Equation (80) and in Britton [5], Ch. 8. Moreover, setting all diffusion constants to zero (and assuming c0∗=0c_{0}^{*}=0 as well as constant y0∗y_{0}^{*}) leads to the usual spatially homogeneous reduction as given in (2.5).
As far as the authors know, this reduced system has not appeared in the literature so far. The numerical simulations in Section 4 indicate convergence.

3.3.2 Irreversible case with δc∗−δe∗=𝒪⁡(1)\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*}=\mathcal{O}(1)

In this case the reduction is given by

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s−k1​k2​y∗​sk1​s+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}y^{*}s}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.12)
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗+δ​Δ​(k1​y∗​sk1​s+k−1+k2),\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\delta\Delta\left(\frac{k_{1}y^{*}s}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\right), in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.13)

on the asymptotic slow manifold

𝒱={(s,c∗,y∗)∈ℝ+3,c∗=k1​s​y∗k1​s+k−1+k2}.\mathcal{V}=\left\{(s,c^{*},y^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{+},\ c^{*}=\frac{k_{1}sy^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\right\}.

The appropriate initial values are as before (also following from Proposition A.3).
This case may be said to correspond to the one mentioned but not treated in Kalachev et al. [14]; there seems to be no discussion of this in the literature. Note that now the equations for ss and y∗y^{*} are fully coupled; this is a more complex situation than before. Again, numerical simulations (Section 4) are in good agreement with the reduction.

3.4 The reversible case

We will determine a reduced system for the reversible Michaelis-Menten reaction with diffusion, i.e.,

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s+(k1​s+k−1)​c∗−k1​s​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s+(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c^{*}-k_{1}sy^{*}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega
∂τc∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}c^{*} =δc∗​Δ​c∗−ε−1​[(k1​s+k−1+k−2​p+k2)​c∗+(k1​s+k−2​p)​y∗],\displaystyle=\delta_{c}^{*}\Delta c^{*}-\varepsilon^{-1}[(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{-2}p+k_{2})c^{*}+(k_{1}s+k_{-2}p)y^{*}], in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗+δ​Δ​c∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\delta\Delta c^{*}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega
∂τp\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}p =δp∗​Δ​p+(k−2​p+k2)​c∗−k−2​p​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{p}^{*}\Delta p+(k_{-2}p+k_{2})c^{*}-k_{-2}py^{*}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega

Here we choose the same scaling as in (3.5)–(3.7) and additionally we let δp=ε​δp∗\delta_{p}=\varepsilon\delta_{p}^{*}. If δc∗−δe∗=𝒪⁡(ε)\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) then we get

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s−(k1​k2​s−k−1​k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s-\frac{(k_{1}k_{2}s-k_{-1}k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.14)
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.15)
∂τp\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}p =δp∗​Δ​p+(k1​k2​s−k−1​k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{p}^{*}\Delta p+\frac{(k_{1}k_{2}s-k_{-1}k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.16)

on the asymptotic slow manifold

𝒱={(s,c∗,y∗,p)∈ℝ+4,c∗=(k1​s+k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2}.\mathcal{V}=\left\{(s,c^{*},y^{*},p)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}_{+},\ c^{*}=\frac{(k_{1}s+k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\right\}.

Note that (3.15) is uncoupled from the remaining system. In case δc∗−δe∗=𝒪⁡(1)\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*}=\mathcal{O}(1) we get

∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs∗​Δ​s−(k1​k2​s−k−1​k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}^{*}\Delta s-\frac{(k_{1}k_{2}s-k_{-1}k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.17)
∂τy∗\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}y^{*} =δe∗​Δ​y∗+δ​Δ​((k1​s+k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2),\displaystyle=\delta_{e}^{*}\Delta y^{*}+\delta\Delta\left(\frac{(k_{1}s+k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\right), in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.18)
∂τp\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}p =δp∗​Δ​p+(k1​k2​s−k−1​k−2​p)​y∗k1​s+k−2​p+k−1+k2,\displaystyle=\delta_{p}^{*}\Delta p+\frac{(k_{1}k_{2}s-k_{-1}k_{-2}p)y^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-2}p+k_{-1}+k_{2}}, in ​(0,T)×Ω\displaystyle\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega (3.19)

on the same asymptotic slow manifold, but here one has a fully coupled system for ss, y∗y^{*} and pp.
The proofs follow from Proposition A.4. In both settings, appropriate initial values are given by (s~0,y~0∗,p~0)=(s0,y0∗,p0)(\tilde{s}_{0},\tilde{y}_{0}^{*},\tilde{p}_{0})=\left(s_{0},y_{0}^{*},p_{0}\right).
Again, setting all diffusion constants to zero (and assuming c0∗=p0=0c_{0}^{*}=p_{0}=0 as well as constant y0∗y_{0}^{*} and s0s_{0}) leads to s⁡(τ,x)+p⁡(τ,x)=s0s(\tau,x)+p(\tau,x)=s_{0} and thus to the usual reduction as given in (2.6).

4 Numerical simulations

In the following we will provide numerical results that are in good agreement with the reduction given above. The solutions have been obtained using MATLAB’s pdepe function. This function solves an initial-boundary value problem for spatially one-dimensional systems of parabolic and elliptic partial differential equations in the self-adjoint form

C⁡(x,t,u,∂xu)​∂tu=x−m​∂x(xm​F​(x,t,u,∂xu))+S⁡(x,t,u,∂xu).C(x,t,u,\partial_{x}u)\partial_{t}u=x^{-m}\partial_{x}(x^{m}F(x,t,u,\partial_{x}u))+S(x,t,u,\partial_{x}u).

In our case, m=0m=0 and CC is the identity matrix. Furthermore, in the case of system (3.5)–(3.7), using the unknown u=(s,c∗,y∗)Tu=(s,c^{*},y^{*})^{T}, the flux FF and the source SS become

F=(δs​∂xsδc∗​∂xc∗δe∗​∂xy∗+δ​∂xc∗),S=((k1​s+k−1)​c∗−k1​s​y∗ε−1​(k1​s+k−1+k2)​c∗+ε−1​k1​s​y∗0).F=\begin{pmatrix}\delta_{s}\partial_{x}s\\ \delta_{c}^{*}\partial_{x}c^{*}\\ \delta_{e}^{*}\partial_{x}y^{*}+\delta\partial_{x}c^{*}\end{pmatrix},\quad S=\begin{pmatrix}(k_{1}s+k_{-1})c^{*}-k_{1}sy^{*}\\ \varepsilon^{-1}(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})c^{*}+\varepsilon^{-1}k_{1}sy^{*}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}.

The reduced system (3.12)–(3.13), using the unknown u=(s,y∗)Tu=(s,y^{*})^{T}, the flux FF and the source SS become

F=(δs​∂xsδ​k1​y​(k−1+k2)(k1​s+k−1+k2)2​∂xs+(δ​k1​sk1​s+k−1+δe∗)​∂xy∗),S=(k1​k2​s​y∗k1​s+k−1+k20).F=\begin{pmatrix}\delta_{s}\partial_{x}s\\ \frac{\delta k_{1}y(k_{-1}+k_{2})}{(k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2})^{2}}\partial_{x}s+(\frac{\delta k_{1}s}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}}+\delta_{e}^{*})\partial_{x}y^{*}\end{pmatrix},\quad S=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{k_{1}k_{2}sy^{*}}{k_{1}s+k_{-1}+k_{2}}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}.

As boundary conditions, we use homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, i.e., for each unknown we set the spatial derivative equal to zero at the boundary.

The pdepe function uses a self-adjoint finite difference semi-discretization in space, and solves the obtained system ordinary differential equations by the implicit, adaptive multistep solver ode15s. In all our experiments we have set the tolerances to values below the accuracy we intend to observe (absolute tolerance 10−1410^{-14}, relative tolerance 10−1010^{-10}). We have used 100 equidistant grid cells.

Figure 1 shows the initial condition we have used; a step function in ss, a smooth cosine profile for cc, and a cosine profile with an additional Gaussian bump for yy. We have set δs=δe=k1=k−1=k2=1\delta_{s}=\delta_{e}=k_{1}=k_{-1}=k_{2}=1 and δc=2\delta_{c}=2 (so δ=1\delta=1; see case 3.3.2).

Figure 2 shows the solutions at time T=0.005T=0.005 for ε=1.0\varepsilon=1.0. Already, one can see that the concentration ss is described well by the reduced system, whereas we see a discrepancy in yy. For ε=0.0001\varepsilon=0.0001, shown in Figure 3, to the eye there is no difference between the solutions of the original and the reduced systems. In Figure 4 we investigate the convergence of the solution of the full system to the solution of the reduced system. The error is measured in the L∞L^{\infty} norm in all three solution components. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, we observe rather clean first-order convergence in double-logarithmic plot. Finally, we also set δc=1\delta_{c}=1 (so δ=0\delta=0; see case 3.3.1) and measure in Figure 5 and Figure 6 again the error. This confirms what the theory has predicted.

5 Concluding remarks

  • •

    As already noted, we do not discuss convergence results. But it is easy to see that the uniform bound for y∗y^{*} implies that cc converges uniformly to 0 as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Moreover, up to taking a subsequence, c∗:=ε−1​cc^{*}:=\varepsilon^{-1}c and y∗y^{*} converge weakly∗\text{weakly}^{*} in C0C^{0} and weakly in LpL^{p} for all 1<p<∞1<p<\infty. This may be a starting point for a convergence proof.

  • •

    As already mentioned, this above reductions can be obtained only after a degenerate scaling of certain variables; then a Tikhonov-Fenichel reduction is applicable. (The corresponding scaling by Heineken et al. [12] in the ODE case is convenient, but not necessary.) This may also be the underlying reason why the approach by Yannacopoulos et al. [25] was not directly applicable to the given setting. The scaled quantities y∗y^{*} and c∗c^{*} can be seen as first order approximations of yy and ss of the solution of (3.2)–(3.4) (with respect to the assumptions regarding slow diffusion and small total initial enzyme concentration) where the zero order terms are equal to zero. The effect of degenerate scalings in general is investigated in a forthcoming paper [18].

  • •

    A reduction similar to the one above was already given in the dissertation [16], but it was based on writing the system in (s,e,c,p)(s,e,c,p) and scaling both e=ε​e∗e=\varepsilon e^{*} and c=ε​c∗c=\varepsilon c^{*}. The reduced system is equivalent to the reduced system given here. We chose to change the variables to (s,c,y,p)(s,c,y,p) in order to emphasize the resemblance to the non-diffusive case which is otherwise lost.

  • •

    It is also possible to only scale yy instead of both cc and yy (and still obtain that cc will be of order ε\varepsilon). But there are some disadvantages: The computation of the reduced system gets more involved as the results of [8] cannot be used directly. Moreover, we only get a zero order approximation to the slow manifold, given by c=0c=0.

  • •

    Different QSS assumptions are also being discussed in the literature. Various choices of small rate constants can be found in [8, 16]; for example the assumptions of slow product formation (k2=ε​k2∗k_{2}=\varepsilon k_{2}^{*}) and slow diffusion (δz=ε​δz∗​ for ​z=s,e,c,p\delta_{z}=\varepsilon\delta_{z}^{*}\text{ for }z=s,e,c,p) as well as only slow product formation are discussed.
    Moreover, the assumption of slow complex formation (k1=ε​k1∗k_{1}=\varepsilon k_{1}^{*} and k−2=ε​k−2∗k_{-2}=\varepsilon k_{-2}^{*}) and slow diffusion can be discussed by employing the method developed in [8]. A reduced system is given by

    ∂τs\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}s =δs​Δ​s−k1​k2k−1+k2​s​e+k−1​k−2k−1+k2​e​p\displaystyle=\delta_{s}\Delta s-\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{-1}+k_{2}}se+\frac{k_{-1}k_{-2}}{k_{-1}+k_{2}}ep
    ∂τe\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}e =δe​Δ​e\displaystyle=\delta_{e}\Delta e
    ∂τp\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}p =δp​Δ​p+k1​k2k−1+k2​s​e−k−1​k−2k−1+k2​e​p\displaystyle=\delta_{p}\Delta p+\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{-1}+k_{2}}se-\frac{k_{-1}k_{-2}}{k_{-1}+k_{2}}ep

    on the slow manifold defined by c=0c=0. This corresponds to the convergence results of Bothe and Pierre [2] and Bisi et al. [1] for a related system which is defined by the reaction A1+A2⇌A3⇌A4+A5A_{1}+A_{2}\rightleftharpoons A_{3}\rightleftharpoons A_{4}+A_{5}. (Note that the latter reaction is easier to analyze, due to the structure of the conservation laws; see Eliaš [6]). In all cases, the numerical results are in good agreement with the reduction.

  • •

    By analogous methods one can derive a reduction given the assumption of small total initial enzyme concentration, but with fast diffusive terms. Scaling again y=ε​y∗y=\varepsilon y^{*} and c=ε​c∗c=\varepsilon c^{*} and using results of [16] one obtains the classical reduction: the fast diffusion yields a homogenization of the concentrations, enzyme and complex are in QSS and the reduced dynamics of the substrate are described by (2.5) (again, the reduction is in good agreement with numerical results). We omit details here.

Appendix A Appendix: Computations and proofs

Here we collect, for the reader’s convenience, some known results and facts, and we present the proofs of some of the main results in Section 3 in detail, sketching the remaining ones.

A.1 Tikhonov-Fenichel reduction of ODEs

We first recall some results from [10]. Consider a polynomial or rational system

x˙=h⁡(x,ε)=h(0)​(x)+ε​h(1)​(x)+⋯,x∈ℝm,ε>0,\dot{x}=h(x,\varepsilon)=h^{(0)}(x)+\varepsilon h^{(1)}(x)+\cdots,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\quad\varepsilon>0, (A.1)

and in addition assume that there exists x0x_{0} in the zero set 𝒱⁡(h(0))\mathcal{V}(h^{(0)}) such that rank⁡D​h(0)​(x)=r<m\rank Dh^{(0)}(x)=r<m for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathbb{R}^{m} near x0x_{0}. We denote by 𝒱\mathcal{V} the irreducible component of 𝒱⁡(h(0))\mathcal{V}(h^{(0)}) which contains x0x_{0}. By the implicit function theorem, there is a (Zariski-open) neighborhood UU of x0x_{0} such that 𝒱∩U\mathcal{V}\cap U is a (m−r)(m-r)-dimensional submanifold.

Proposition A.1.

(See [10], Theorem 1.) Assume furthermore that

ℝm=ker⁡D​h(0)​(x)⊕im⁡D​h(0)​(x)\mathbb{R}^{m}=\ker Dh^{(0)}(x)\oplus\im Dh^{(0)}(x)

for all x∈𝒱∩Ux\in\mathcal{V}\cap U, and that there exists ν>0\nu>0 such that all nonzero eigenvalues of D​h(0)​(x)Dh^{(0)}(x), x∈𝒱x\in\mathcal{V}, have real part ≤−ν\leq-\nu. Then the following hold.

  1. (a)

    There exist rational maps

    P:ℝm→ℝm×randμ:ℝm→ℝrP\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\quad\text{and}\quad\mu\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{r}

    which are regular in x0x_{0}, with rank⁡P⁡(x0)=rank⁡D​μ​(x0)=r\rank P(x_{0})=\rank D\mu(x_{0})=r, such that the identity

    h(0)​(x)=P⁡(x)​μ​(x)h^{(0)}(x)=P(x)\mu(x)

    of rational functions holds. Moreover, the zero set YY of μ\mu satisfies Y∩U~=𝒱∩U~Y\cap\widetilde{U}=\mathcal{V}\cap\widetilde{U} in some Zariski-open neighborhood U~\widetilde{U} of x0x_{0}.

  2. (b)

    The system

    x′=q⁡(x):=Q⁡(x)⋅h(1)​(x)x^{\prime}=q(x):=Q(x)\cdot h^{(1)}(x) (A.2)

    with

    Q⁡(x):=Im−P⁡(x)​(D​μ​(x)​P​(x))−1​D​μ​(x),Q(x):=I_{m}-P(x)(D\mu(x)P(x))^{-1}D\mu(x),

    (in slow time τ=ε​t\tau=\varepsilon t) is defined in x0x_{0}, and the manifold Y∩U~Y\cap\widetilde{U} is an invariant set of (A.2).

  3. (c)

    There exists T>0T>0 and a neighborhood U∗⊂UU^{*}\subset U of YY such that, for any τ0\tau_{0} with 0<τ0<T0<\tau_{0}<T, solutions of

    x′=ε−1​h​(x,ε)x^{\prime}=\varepsilon^{-1}h(x,\varepsilon)

    starting in U∗U^{*} converge uniformly on [τ0,T][\tau_{0},T] to solutions of the reduced system (A.2) on YY as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

We call (A.2) the Tikhonov-Fenichel reduction of (A.1). In order to apply this reduction, one also needs to know the appropriate initial value on YY. This was basically settled by Fenichel [7] Theorem 9.1 and was discussed in detail for the given particular setting in [10] (see also the references given there). We briefly summarize: By [10] Proposition 2, the system x˙=h(0)​(x)\dot{x}=h^{(0)}(x) admits m−rm-r first integrals in a neighborhood of x0x_{0}. Moreover, the intersection of a common level set of the first integrals with 𝒱⁡(h(0))\mathcal{V}(h^{(0)}) consists (locally) of a single point. Thus, to project the initial values of system (A.1) to (A.2), choose the corresponding intersection point.
In general it will not be possible to determine the first integrals explicitly (see [10] Remark 6 for details on an approximation by Taylor series), but for Michaelis-Menten in this particular setting the first integrals are easily determined and the projected initial values (for the relevant variables ss, y∗y^{*} and pp) are identical to the original ones.

A.2 Discretization

Here we briefly review the spatial discretization procedure, and some properties of the discretized system; see [8] and [16]. For the sake of simplicity we assume that Ω=(0,L)\Omega=(0,L) is a real interval. (When Ω=(0,L1)×(0,L2)×⋯×(0,Ln)⊆ℝn\Omega=(0,L_{1})\times(0,L_{2})\times\cdots\times(0,L_{n})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} holds, a similar discretization with obvious adjustments can be carried out. Note that the special choice of Ω\Omega is relevant only for the derivation of the reduced PDE system.)
Let L=N​ρL=N\rho, where ρ\rho is the mesh size. We subdivide Ω\Omega in compartments Ωα=((α−1)​ρ,α​ρ),\Omega_{\alpha}=\left((\alpha-1)\rho,\alpha\rho\right), with 1≤α≤N1\leq\alpha\leq N, and we identify α\alpha with the compartment Ωα\Omega_{\alpha}. Define zαz_{\alpha} as the concentration of species ZZ at the center xαx_{\alpha} of compartment α\alpha (with Z=S,E,C,PZ=S,E,C,P), and let

z^:=(zα)1≤α≤N∈ℝN.\widehat{z}:=(z_{\alpha})_{1\leq\alpha\leq N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}.

We choose a central difference discretization of the Laplacian, i.e.

𝒟α​z^=zα−1−2​zα+zα+1ρ2,1≤α≤N.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}\widehat{z}=\frac{z_{\alpha-1}-2z_{\alpha}+z_{\alpha+1}}{\rho^{2}},\quad 1\leq\alpha\leq N.

To incorporate the Neumann boundary conditions, we set z0=z1z_{0}=z_{1} and zN+1=zNz_{N+1}=z_{N}.
The discretization of (2.7)–(2.10) is given by

s˙α\displaystyle\dot{s}_{\alpha} =δs​𝒟α​s^−k1​sα​eα+k−1​cα,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{s}-k_{1}s_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}+k_{-1}c_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.3)
e˙α\displaystyle\dot{e}_{\alpha} =δe​𝒟α​e^−k1​sα​eα+(k−1+k2)​cα−k−2​eα​pα,\displaystyle=\delta_{e}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{e}-k_{1}s_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}+(k_{-1}+k_{2})c_{\alpha}-k_{-2}e_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.4)
c˙α\displaystyle\dot{c}_{\alpha} =δc​𝒟α​c^+k1​sα​eα−(k−1+k2)​cα+k−2​eα​pα,\displaystyle=\delta_{c}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{c}+k_{1}s_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}-(k_{-1}+k_{2})c_{\alpha}+k_{-2}e_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.5)
p˙α\displaystyle\dot{p}_{\alpha} =δp​𝒟α​p^+k2​cα−k−2​eα​pα,\displaystyle=\delta_{p}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{p}+k_{2}c_{\alpha}-k_{-2}e_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.6)

with initial values

sα​(0)=sα,0:=s0​(xα),eα​(0)=eα,0:=e0​(xα),\displaystyle s_{\alpha}(0)=s_{\alpha,0}:=s_{0}(x_{\alpha}),\quad e_{\alpha}(0)=e_{\alpha,0}:=e_{0}(x_{\alpha}),
cα​(0)=cα,0:=c0​(xα),pα​(0)=pα,0:=p0​(xα).\displaystyle c_{\alpha}(0)=c_{\alpha,0}:=c_{0}(x_{\alpha}),\quad p_{\alpha}(0)=p_{\alpha,0}:=p_{0}(x_{\alpha}).

We will also make use of the total enzyme concentrations

y^:=e^+c^\widehat{y}:=\widehat{e}+\widehat{c}

and the discretized diffusion matrix 𝒟\cal D, which in dimension one has the form

𝒟:=(𝒟α)1≤α≤N=1ρ2​(−111−21⋱⋱⋱⋱⋱⋱1−211−1).\mathcal{D}:=\left(\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}\right)_{1\leq\alpha\leq N}=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\ 1&-2&1\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots\\ &&&1&-2&1\\ &&&&1&-1\end{pmatrix}.

(In spatial dimension n>1n>1, the discretized diffusion matrix 𝒟\mathcal{D} for (0,L1)×⋯×(0,Ln)(0,L_{1})\times\cdots\times(0,L_{n}) is of different form but in any case it is a so-called WW-matrix, i.e. the sum of all rows is equal to zero and all off-diagonal elements are nonnegative.)
Our fundamental assumptions for the discretized system correspond to those in Subsection 3.3; they are as follows:

  1. (i)

    Diffusion is slow, thus one may scale

    δs=εδs∗,δc=εδc∗,,δe=εδe∗,δp=εδp∗\delta_{s}=\varepsilon\delta_{s}^{*},\quad\delta_{c}=\varepsilon\delta_{c}^{*},\quad,\delta_{e}=\varepsilon\delta_{e}^{*},\quad\delta_{p}=\varepsilon\delta_{p}^{*} (A.7)

    with a small parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0.

  2. (ii)

    The initial concentrations of enzyme and complex are small of order ε\varepsilon in every compartment; hence there is a constant E>0E>0 such that eα,0≤E⋅εe_{\alpha,0}\leq E\cdot\varepsilon and cα,0≤E⋅εc_{\alpha,0}\leq E\cdot\varepsilon for all α\alpha.

Requirement (ii) is less restrictive than the corresponding one for the PDE system, since the conditions refer only to t=0t=0. Actually, for the ODE system after discretization the property for t>0t>0 follows automatically, and we will prove this and some other basic properties for the discretized system next.

Lemma A.2.
  1. (a)

    For every x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N} one has ∑α𝒟α​(x)=0\sum_{\alpha}{\cal D}_{\alpha}(x)=0.

  2. (b)

    Solutions with nonnegative initial values are nonnegative for all t≥0t\geq 0.

  3. (c)

    One has

    ∑α(sα+eα+2​cα+pα)=∑α(sα,0+eα,0+2​cα,0+pα,0)\sum_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha}+e_{\alpha}+2c_{\alpha}+p_{\alpha})=\sum_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha,0}+e_{\alpha,0}+2c_{\alpha,0}+p_{\alpha,0})

    for every t≥0t\geq 0; in particular every component of the solution is bounded.

  4. (d)

    There is a constant C>0C>0 such that yα=eα+cα≤C⋅εy_{\alpha}=e_{\alpha}+c_{\alpha}\leq C\cdot\varepsilon for all t≥0t\geq 0, 1≤α≤N1\leq\alpha\leq N.

Proof.

Part (a) reflects the property of the discretized diffusion matrix 𝒟\cal D that the sum of its rows equals zero. Part (b) is a consequence of the fact that off-diagonal elements of 𝒟\cal D are nonnegative, hence the rate of change for every variable zαz_{\alpha} is nonnegative whenever zα=0z_{\alpha}=0. Part (c) follows from (a) and (A.3) – (A.6), and part (d) follows from

∑α(eα+cα)=∑α(eα,0+cα,0)≤2​N​E⋅ε.\sum_{\alpha}(e_{\alpha}+c_{\alpha})=\sum_{\alpha}(e_{\alpha,0}+c_{\alpha,0})\leq 2NE\cdot\varepsilon.

∎

In view of part (d) of the Lemma, the scaling

yα=ε​yα∗​ and ​cα=ε​cα∗,1≤α≤Ny_{\alpha}=\varepsilon y_{\alpha}^{*}\text{ and }c_{\alpha}=\varepsilon c_{\alpha}^{*},\quad 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.8)

is consistent; i.e., all yα∗y_{\alpha}^{*} and cα∗c_{\alpha}^{*} remain bounded in ε\varepsilon for t≥0t\geq 0 whenever assumption (ii) holds.

For the irreversible system (thus k−2=0k_{-2}=0) one has

since the equations for p^\widehat{p} may be omitted. Rewriting the system with y^=e^+c^\widehat{y}=\widehat{e}+\widehat{c}, we get

s˙α\displaystyle\dot{s}_{\alpha} =δs​𝒟α​s^−k1​sα​(yα−cα)+k−1​cα,\displaystyle=\delta_{s}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{s}-k_{1}s_{\alpha}(y_{\alpha}-c_{\alpha})+k_{-1}c_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.12)
c˙α\displaystyle\dot{c}_{\alpha} =δc​𝒟α​c^+k1​sα​(yα−cα)−(k−1+k2)​cα,\displaystyle=\delta_{c}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{c}+k_{1}s_{\alpha}(y_{\alpha}-c_{\alpha})-(k_{-1}+k_{2})c_{\alpha}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.13)

With the scalings (A.7) and (A.8), system (A.12)– (A.14) becomes

s˙α\displaystyle\dot{s}_{\alpha} =ε​δs∗​𝒟α​s^+ε⁡(k1​sα+k−1)​cα∗−ε​k1​sα​yα∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{s}^{*}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{s}+\varepsilon(k_{1}s_{\alpha}+k_{-1})c^{*}_{\alpha}-\varepsilon k_{1}s_{\alpha}y_{\alpha}^{*}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N (A.15)

where δ=δc∗−δe∗\delta=\delta_{c}^{*}-\delta_{e}^{*} as in (3.8). The main result in Section 3.3 is a direct consequence of the following Proposition; note that the reduced ODE system is the spatial discretization of (3.10) – (3.11) resp. (3.12) – (3.13).

Here we sketch the argument leading to the reduction in Subsection 3.4. This is parallel to the irreversible case, hence we will present fewer details. Using the scalings (A.7) and (A.8) and rewriting the system in terms of c^∗\widehat{c}^{*} and y^∗\widehat{y}^{*}, (A.3)–(A.6) becomes

y˙α∗\displaystyle\dot{y}^{*}_{\alpha} =ε​δe∗​𝒟α​y^∗+ε​δ​𝒟α​c^∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{e}^{*}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{y}^{*}+\varepsilon\delta{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{c}^{*}, 1≤α≤N\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N
p˙α\displaystyle\dot{p}_{\alpha} =ε​δp∗​𝒟α​p^+ε⁡(k2+k−2​pα)​cα∗−ε​k−2​pα​yα∗,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\delta_{p}^{*}{\cal D}_{\alpha}\widehat{p}+\varepsilon(k_{2}+k_{-2}p_{\alpha})c_{\alpha}^{*}-\varepsilon k_{-2}p_{\alpha}y_{\alpha}^{*}, 1≤α≤N.\displaystyle 1\leq\alpha\leq N.

μ=(−(k1​sα+k−1+k2+k−2​pα)​cα∗+(k1​sα+k−2​pα)​yα∗)1≤α≤N\mu=\big(-(k_{1}s_{\alpha}+k_{-1}+k_{2}+k_{-2}p_{\alpha})c^{*}_{\alpha}+(k_{1}s_{\alpha}+k_{-2}p_{\alpha})y_{\alpha}^{*}\big)_{1\leq\alpha\leq N}
